opus-5.5.text:
Kaiming is someone I've learned a tremendous amount from, and the writing piece is a big part of that. The first thing I'd point to is clarity. He treats a paper as a piece of communication, not just a record of experiments. Before writing, he has a very sharp sense of the one core message the paper should deliver, and everything is organized around it. If a paragraph, a table, or even a sentence doesn't serve that message, it gets cut.

The second thing is simplicity. Many of his best-known works, like ResNet, have ideas that look almost obvious in hindsight. That's partly because the idea is genuinely simple, but also because he works very hard to present it that way. He resists making a method look more complicated than it is to seem impressive. Writing a simple idea so that it feels inevitable is actually much harder than writing a complicated one.

Third, he's extremely careful and honest about experiments. The ablations are designed to answer the questions a skeptical reader would ask, and he doesn't oversell. Claims are scoped to what the evidence supports. That builds trust, and I think it's one reason his papers age well.

And finally, the craftsmanship in the details: figures that explain the idea at a glance, consistent notation, very deliberate wording, many rounds of revision. Working with him, you see he'll rewrite the introduction again and again until the logic flows naturally. It taught me that writing isn't the last step after research is done. It's part of thinking clearly about the research itself.

r001.rationale: The response mentions many rounds of revision and repeated rewriting, but does not say Kaiming finishes papers early enough to polish them before the deadline.

fable-5.1.text:
What I admire most is how much he cares about clarity, almost to an obsessive degree. When we wrote ResNeXt together, and later when I watched him work on other papers, the thing that struck me was that he treats writing as part of the research itself, not something you do at the end to package the results.

He has this principle that a paper should have one idea, and everything in the paper should serve that idea. If a sentence or a figure doesn't help the reader understand the core message, it gets cut. He would rewrite the same paragraph many times, not to make it sound fancy, but to make it simpler. He often says that if a reader can't grasp the main point from the abstract and the first figure, the paper has already failed.

The other thing is honesty in presentation. He doesn't oversell. The ablation tables in his papers are there because he actually wants to understand why something works, not just to show it works. I remember him insisting on including experiments that didn't look impressive, because they answered a question a careful reader would naturally ask. That kind of intellectual honesty builds trust, and I think it's a big reason his papers have had such lasting influence.

And finally, he writes for the reader who will come five years later, not for the reviewer next month. That changed how I think about my own work. Now when I write, I ask myself: will a student picking this up years from now still understand what we were trying to say, and why it mattered? That's something I learned directly from him.

r001.rationale: The response says Kaiming repeatedly rewrote paragraphs, but does not say he completed papers early or that this left time for polishing before the deadline.

astra-6.text: What I admire is the clarity. He has a very good sense of what the central idea of a paper is, and he organizes the explanation around that. You don’t want the reader to merely follow the technical details; you want them to understand why the question matters and why the solution makes sense. That takes a lot of thought. A paper can look simple when you read it, but making it that clear is actually very difficult. That’s something I really appreciate about his approach.

sol-6.1.text:
What I admire is how much effort Kaiming puts into making an idea clear. The paper can feel simple when you read it, but that simplicity takes a lot of work. You have to understand what the central contribution really is, what evidence supports it, and what you can leave out.

He’s very good at building that logical thread so the reader can follow the reasoning without getting lost in details. I think that’s an important lesson: writing isn’t just presenting the research after it’s finished. It’s also a way to test whether you really understand what you’ve done.
